    if b<a: return 1-b/a

strengths: The multiclass extension is well motivated: equalized odds should distinguish different types of prediction errors. The mixture formulation retains a meaningful interpretation as minimum nuisance mass, and the relationship to Sabato and Yom-Tov (2020) is clearly acknowledged.

Theorem 4.1, the analytical lower bound in Eq. (7), and monotonicity under label merging provide a coherent mathematical foundation. The greedy initialization makes useful use of the tractable binary problem.

Distinguishing known confusion matrices from aggregate-only observations addresses practically different auditing settings. The minDCP formulation clearly expresses the smallest disparity compatible with the available marginal statistics.

Experiments cover multiple prediction tasks, three classifier families, and two individual-level datasets. Greedy initialization with local optimization generally improves the reported upper bounds, with particularly tight intervals on several Natality tasks. Algorithmic appendices and a code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The accuracy claim for aggregate-only auditing is insufficiently supported. Although Section 7 claims tight upper/lower bounds in both regimes, Tables 2 and 7–10 report local upper bounds on minDCP without its corresponding lower bounds or optimality gaps. Comparing these values with the original classifier's DCP interval does not establish proximity to minDCP. A large upper bound cannot certify unavoidable disparity, and differences between upper bounds need not reflect differences between the underlying minima. This substantially weakens the interpretation of the election and education experiments.

The assertion that distribution-estimation error transfers to at most the same DCP error is neither proved nor generally correct under standard total variation distance. For equally weighted groups, changing identical binary prediction rates of 0.5 to 0.49 and 0.51 changes the joint distribution by total variation 0.01 but increases DCP from zero to 1/51, approximately 0.0196. This example can be repeated across true labels. Consequently, population-level guarantees require an explicit stability analysis and statistical uncertainty treatment. Clipping confusion-matrix entries and modifying prediction marginals also change the target problem; existing sampling noise does not automatically preserve bound validity.

Appendix D contains a concrete error in its convergence justification. The function called eta_convex in Eq. (18) is not jointly convex in its two optimization arguments: on the branch b<a, a²−ab has an indefinite Hessian. Figure 4 therefore does not demonstrate convergence on the claimed convex problem. The applicability of the cited SLP convergence results to the implemented constraint removal and step-size rules also needs justification. Feasible objective values can remain useful upper bounds without these convergence claims.

The optimization evaluation lacks runtime/scaling measurements and comparisons with alternative constrained optimizers. Even a simple baseline is missing: choosing the identity confusion matrix as the common baseline gives DCP no greater than classification error. In Table 1, the eight-class upper bound of 23.61% exceeds the reported error of 22.61%. Including this baseline and globally solved small instances would better establish optimization quality, particularly where reported bound ratios exceed two.

The claimed advantages over difference- and ratio-based fairness measures need concrete supporting comparisons. In particular, weighting by group and true-label frequencies necessarily reduces the contribution of disparities confined to rare groups or labels. The broad suggestion that DCP avoids discounting rare-label differences therefore needs qualification. Its nuisance-mass interpretation also should not be conflated with identifying individuals who actually experienced unfair treatment.

Reproduction from the manuscript remains difficult because preprocessing, evaluation splits, target attribute names for the repeated Census rows, and aggregate-optimizer initialization and stopping settings are incompletely specified. Minor reporting inconsistencies also need correction: for example, Section 7.1 states a maximum Natality bound ratio of 1.58, while Table 1 reports 1.71.
